### [Optimal Timing for Superintelligence: Mundane Considerations for Existing People](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2trvf5byng7caPsyx/optimal-timing-for-superintelligence-mundane-considerations)

**来源**: LessWrong - AI

**摘要**: Published on February 12, 2026 5:06 PM GMT<br /><br /><p>[<i>Sorry about the lengthiness of this post. &nbsp;I recommend not fixating too much on all the specific numbers and the formal apparatus. &nbsp;Originally the plan was to also analyze optimal timing from an impersonal (xrisk-minimization) perspective; but to prevent the text from ballooning even more, that topic was set aside for future work (which might never get done). &nbsp;But I should at least emphasize that there are other important factors, not covered here, that would need to be taken into account if one wishes to determine which timeline would be best all things considered.</i>]</p><p>[<i>Working paper.</i><span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref7epfhhb5vpp"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn7epfhhb5vpp">[1]</a></sup></span><i>&nbsp; Version 1.0. &nbsp;&nbsp;</i><a href="https://nickbostrom.com/optimal.pdf"><i>Canonical link to future revised version of this paper</i></a>.]</p><hr /><h1>Abstract</h1><p>Developing superintelligence is not like playing Russian roulette; it is more like undergoing risky surgery for a condition that will otherwise prove fatal. &nbsp;We examine optimal timing from a person-affecting stance (and set aside simulation hypotheses and other arcane considerations). &nbsp;Models incorporating safety progress, temporal discounting, quality-of-life differentials, and concave QALY utilities suggest that even high catastrophe probabilities are often worth accepting. &nbsp;Prioritarian weighting further shortens timelines. &nbsp;For many parameter settings, the optimal strategy would involve moving quickly to AGI capability, then pausing briefly before full deployment: swift to harbor, slow to berth. &nbsp;But poorly implemented pauses could do more harm than good.</p><h1>Introduction</h1><p>Some have called for a pause or permanent halt to AI development, on grounds that it would otherwise lead to AGI and superintelligence, which would pose intolerable dangers, including existential risks. &nbsp;For&nbsp;instance, Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares argue in their recent book <i>If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies</i>&nbsp;that nations should enforce a global ban on advanced AI and the computational infrastructure to support it, and on research into improved AI algorithms.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-1"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-1">[2]</a></sup></span>&nbsp; These authors are extremely pessimistic about the prospects of aligned superintelligent AI, regarding its advent as an almost certain doom. &nbsp;In their view, creating superintelligence would be far worse than subjecting all of humanity to a universal death sentence.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-2"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-2">[3]</a></sup></span>&nbsp; Others have argued that even a much lower level of risk would warrant an indefinite moratorium on AI. &nbsp;Would it not be wildly irresponsible, they ask, to expose our entire species to even a 1-in-10 chance of annihilation?</p><p>However, sound policy analysis must weigh potential benefits alongside the risks&nbsp;of any emerging technology. &nbsp;Yudkowsky and Soares maintain that if anyone builds AGI, everyone dies. &nbsp;One could equally maintain that if <i>nobody</i>&nbsp;builds it, everyone dies. &nbsp;In fact, most people are already dead. &nbsp;The rest of us are on course to follow within a few short decades. &nbsp;For many individuals—such as the elderly and the gravely ill—the end is much closer. &nbsp;Part of the promise of superintelligence is that it might fundamentally change this condition.</p><p>For AGI and superintelligence (we refrain from imposing precise definitions of these terms, as the considerations in this paper don’t depend on exactly how the distinction is drawn), the potential benefits are immense. &nbsp;In particular, sufficiently advanced AI could remove or reduce many other risks to our survival, both as individuals and as a civilization.</p><p>Superintelligence would be able to enormously accelerate advances in biology and medicine—devising cures for all diseases and developing powerful anti-aging and rejuvenation therapies to restore the weak and sick to full youthful vigor.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-3"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-3">[4]</a></sup></span>&nbsp; (There are more radical possibilities beyond this, such as mind uploading, though our argument doesn’t require entertaining those.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-4"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-4">[5]</a></sup></span>) &nbsp;Imagine curing Alzheimer’s disease by regrowing the lost neurons in the patient’s brain. &nbsp;Imagine treating cancer with targeted therapies that eliminate every tumor cell but cause none of the horrible side effects of today’s chemotherapy. &nbsp;Imagine restoring ailing joints and clogged arteries to a pristine youthful condition. &nbsp;These scenarios become realistic and imminent with superintelligence guiding our science.</p><p>Aligned superintelligence could also do much to enhance humanity’s <i>collective safety</i>&nbsp;against global threats. &nbsp;It could advise us on the likely consequences of world-scale decisions, help coordinate efforts to avoid war, counter new bioweapons or other emerging dangers, and generally steer or stabilize various dynamics that might otherwise derail our future.</p><p>In short, if the transition to the era of superintelligence goes well, there is tremendous upside both for saving the lives of currently existing individuals and for safeguarding the long-term survival and flourishing of Earth-originating intelligent life. &nbsp;The choice before us, therefore, is not between a risk-free baseline and a risky AI venture. &nbsp;It is between different risky trajectories, each exposing us to a different set of hazards. &nbsp;Along one path (forgoing superintelligence), 170,000 people die every day of disease, aging, and other tragedies; there is widespread suffering among humans and animals; and we are exposed to some level of ongoing existential risk that looks set to increase (with the emergence of powerful technologies other than AI). &nbsp;The other path (developing superintelligence) introduces unprecedented risks from AI itself, including the possibility of catastrophic misalignment and other failure modes; but it also offers a chance to eliminate or greatly mitigate the baseline threats and misfortunes, and unlock wonderful new levels of flourishing. &nbsp;To decide wisely between these paths, we must compare their complex risk profiles—along with potential upsides—for each of us alive today, and for humanity as a whole.</p><p>With&nbsp;this in mind, it becomes clear (<i>pace</i>&nbsp;Hunt, Yampolskiy, and various other writers) that analogies likening AGI development to a game of Russian roulette are misplaced.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-5"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-5">[6]</a></sup></span>&nbsp; Yes, launching superintelligence entails substantial risk—but a better analogy is a patient with severe heart disease deciding whether to undergo risky surgery.&nbsp; Imagine a patient with advanced coronary artery disease who must weigh the immediate risk of bypass surgery against the ongoing risk of leaving the condition untreated. &nbsp;Without an operation, they might expect to live for several more months, with a gradually increasing daily risk of a fatal cardiac event. &nbsp;The risk of dying on any given day remains small, but it relentlessly accumulates over time. &nbsp;If they opt for surgery, they face a much higher risk of dying immediately on the operating table. &nbsp;However, if the procedure succeeds, the reward is many additional years of life in better health.</p><p>Whether the patient should undergo the operation, and if so <i>when</i>, depends on many variables—their tolerance for risk, their discount rate on future life years, whether a more skillful surgeon is likely to become available at some point, how much better their quality of life would be if the condition is cured, and so on. &nbsp;All these considerations have clear parallels in deciding whether and when to deploy transformative superintelligent AI.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-6"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-6">[7]</a></sup></span></p><p>When we take both sides of the ledger into account, it becomes plausible that our individual life expectancy is <i>higher</i>&nbsp;if superintelligence is developed reasonably soon. &nbsp;Moreover, the life we stand to gain would plausibly be of immensely higher quality than the life we risk forfeiting. &nbsp;This conclusion holds even on highly pessimistic “doomer” assumptions about the probability of misaligned AI causing disaster.</p><h1>Evaluative framework</h1><p>To analyze all the facets of our predicament is possibly infeasible—certainly too complex to attempt in a single paper. &nbsp;However, we can examine some of the tradeoffs through a few different lenses, each providing a view on some of the relevant considerations. &nbsp;By breaking the issue down in this way, we can clarify some aspects of the macrostrategic choices we face, even if a comprehensive evaluation remains out of reach.</p><p>One distinction that may usefully be made is between what we could term <i>mundane</i>&nbsp;and <i>arcane</i>&nbsp;realms of consideration. &nbsp;By the former we refer to the ordinary kinds of secular considerations that most educated modern people would understand and not regard as outlandish or weird (given the postulated technological advances). &nbsp;The latter refers to all the rest—anthropics, simulation theory, aliens, trade between superintelligences, theology, noncausal decision theories, digital minds with moral status, infinite ethics, and whatnot. &nbsp;The arcane is, in the author’s view, relevant and important; but it is harder to get to grips with, and rolling it in upfront would obscure some simpler points that are worth making. &nbsp;In this paper, we therefore limit our purview to mundane considerations (leaving more exotic issues to possibly be addressed in subsequent work).<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-7"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-7">[8]</a></sup></span></p><p>Within either the mundane or arcane domain, we must also decide which evaluative standard to apply. &nbsp;In particular, we may distinguish between a person-affecting perspective, which focuses on the interests of existing people, and an impersonal perspective, which extends consideration to all possible future generations that may or may not come into existence depending on our choices. &nbsp;Individual mortality risks are salient in the person-affecting perspective, whereas existential risks emerge as a central concern in the impersonal perspective. &nbsp;In what follows, we adopt the person-affecting perspective (leaving an analysis from the impersonal perspective for future work).</p><p>We begin by introducing a very simple model. &nbsp;Subsequent sections will explore various complications and elaborations.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-8"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-8">[9]</a></sup></span></p><h1>A simple go/no-go model</h1><p>Suppose that without superintelligence, the average remaining life expectancy is 40&nbsp;years.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-9"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-9">[10]</a></sup></span>&nbsp; With superintelligence, we assume that rejuvenation medicine could reduce mortality rates to a constant level similar to that currently enjoyed by healthy 20-year-olds&nbsp;in developed countries, which corresponds to a life expectancy of around 1,400 years.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-10"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-10">[11]</a></sup></span>&nbsp; This is conservative, since superintelligence could also mitigate many non-aging causes of death—such as infectious diseases, accidents, and suicidal depression. &nbsp;It is also conservative because it ignores more radical possibilities (like mind uploading with periodic backup copies), which could yield vastly longer lifespans.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-11"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-11">[12]</a></sup></span></p><p>Now consider a choice between never launching superintelligence or launching it immediately, where the latter carries an&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">x</span></span></span></span></span></span></span>% risk of immediate universal death. &nbsp;Developing superintelligence increases our life expectancy if and only if:</p><span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage mjpage__block"><span class="mjx-chtml MJXc-display" style="text-align: center;"><span class="mjx-math"><span 2 shows the corresponding thresholds if the gain in life expectancy were only 20 years (so post-AGI life expectancy is 60 years instead of 40)—perhaps a case in which the underlying aging processes for some reason remain unaddressed.</p><p><strong>TABLE 2: Acceptable AI-risk if post-AGI life expectancy is 60 years</strong></p><figure class="table"><table><thead><tr><th>Pre-AGI LE observe that, from a mundane person-affecting perspective—even without a difference in quality of life and with very modest assumptions about superintelligence-enabled life extension—developing superintelligence now would <i>increase</i>&nbsp;expected remaining lifespan&nbsp;even with fairly high levels of AI risk.<span class="footnote-reference" id="fnref-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-12"><sup><a href="https://www.lesswrong.com/feed.xml?view=community-rss&amp;karmaThreshold=30#fn-GrugcNmdFAeTagv7Q-12">[13]</a></sup></span></p><h1>Incorporating time and safety progress</h1><p>The previous section treated the choice as binary: either launch superintelligence now or never launch it at all. &nbsp;In reality, however, we may instead face a timing decision. &nbsp;We may be able to make AGI safer by slowing its development or delaying its deployment, allowing further alignment research (and other precautions) to reduce the risk of catastrophic failure. &nbsp;This introduces a new tradeoff. &nbsp;Launching earlier means accepting a higher level of AI risk; launching later means extending the period during which people continue to die from ordinary causes and remain vulnerable to other background dangers.</p><p>This mirrors the medical analogy introduced earlier. &nbsp;A patient might postpone a risky operation in the hope that a safer method becomes available, but waiting exposes them to the ongoing risk of the underlying disease (and postpones their enjoying a state of improved health).</p><p>To formalize this idea (details in Appendix A), we assume that before AGI, individuals face a constant mortality hazard <i>m0</i>; after a successful launch, this drops to a much lower value <i>m</i>1. &nbsp;We also assume that the probability of catastrophic failure if AI is launched at time <i>t</i>&nbsp;declines gradually as safety work advances. &nbsp;The central question becomes: How long is it worth waiting for additional safety progress?</p><p>Table 3 shows representative “optimal waiting times” under different assumptions about the initial level of AGI risk and the (relative) rate at which that risk is reduced through further safety work. &nbsp;We include some perhaps unrealistically extreme values for initial&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">P</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">doom</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>&nbsp;(at&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">t</span></span><span class="mjx-mo MJXc-space3"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">=</span></span><span class="mjx-mn MJXc-space3"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">0</span></span></span></span></span></span></span>) and rate of safety progress to get a sense of the full space of possibilities.</p><p><strong>TABLE 3: Optimal delay for various initial risks and rates of safety progress</strong></p><figure class="table"><table><tbody><tr><td><strong>Safety Progress</strong></td><td><strong>1%</strong></td><td><strong>5%</strong></td><td><strong>20%</strong></td><td><strong>50%</strong></td><td><strong>80%</strong></td><td><strong>95%</strong></td><td><strong>99%</strong></td></tr><tr><td>No 9.5m</td><td>Wait 11.9m</td><td>Wait 1.1y</td><td>Wait 1.1y</td><td>Wait 1.1y</td></tr></tbody></table></figure><p>We observe&nbsp;a clear pattern.&nbsp; When the initial risk is low, the optimal strategy is to launch AGI as soon as possible—unless safety progress is exceptionally rapid, in which case a brief delay of a couple of months may be warranted. &nbsp;As the initial risk increases, optimal wait times become longer. &nbsp;But unless the starting risk is very high <i>and</i>&nbsp;safety progress is sluggish, the preferred delay remains modest—typically a single-digit number of years.&nbsp; The situation is further illustrated in Figure 1, which shows iso-delay contours across the parameter space.</p><p>Interestingly, both very fast and very slow rates of safety progress favor <i>earlier</i>&nbsp;launch. &nbsp;In the fast-progress case, the risk drops so quickly that there is no need to wait long. &nbsp;In the slow-progress case, waiting yields little benefit, so it is better to act sooner—while the potential gains are still reachable for many. &nbsp;It is intermediate-to-slow progress rates that produce the longest optimal delays: just slow enough that safety improvements accumulate only gradually, but fast enough that waiting still buys some benefit. &nbsp;(There is also a corner case: if the initial risk is extremely high and safety improvements are negligible or non-existent, the model recommends never launching at all.)</p><p>If we measured outcomes in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) rather than raw life-years, we would in most cases become even more impatient to launch. &nbsp;However, in the current model, this effect is modest. &nbsp;The prospect of reducing mortality to that of a healthy 20-year-old already dominates the tradeoff, making the value of the short pre-AGI period relatively insignificant by comparison. &nbsp;What drives the result is the balance between the risk of dying before AGI arrives, and the risk of dying because the launch goes wrong.</p><p><strong>FIGURE 1: Iso-delay contours (cf. Table 3)</strong></p><figure class="image"><img src="https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/2trvf5byng7caPsyx/bxuaibb4ydwdmrjgwn9e" /></figure><h1>Temporal discounting</h1><p>Thus far, we have assumed that future life-years are valued equally regardless of when they occur. &nbsp;In practice, decision-makers often apply a temporal discount rate, which downweights benefits that occur further in the future. &nbsp;Various pragmatic factors that are sometimes baked into an economic discount rate can be set aside here. &nbsp;For example, we should not use the discount rate to account for the fact that we may prefer to frontload good things in our lives on the ground that we might not be around to enjoy them if they are postponed far into the future (since we are modeling mortality risks separately). &nbsp;But decision-makers are sometimes supposed to also have a “pure time preference”, where they simply care less about what happens further into the future, and this is what we will examine here.</p><p>Discounting weakens the incentive to “rush” for the vast long-term life extension that successful AGI might bring. &nbsp;The enormous benefit of gaining centuries of expected life is no longer valued at its full magnitude; whereas the risk of dying soon—either from a misaligned AGI or from current background hazards—remains at nearly full weight. &nbsp;As a result, introducing a discount rate shifts the optimal launch date later.</p><p>Table 4 illustrates the effect of a medium (3%) annual discount rate on optimal AGI timing. &nbsp;(Technical details appear in Appendix B, along with results for other discount rates.)</p><p><strong>TABLE 4: Optimal delay with a 3% annual discount rate</strong></p><figure class="table"><table><tbody><tr><td><strong>Safety progress (0%/yr)</td><td>Launch asap</td><td>Launch asap</td><td>Launch asap</td><td>Never</td><td>Never</td><td>Never</td><td>Never</td></tr><tr><td>Glacial (0.1%/yr)</td><td>Launch asap</td><td>Launch asap</td><td>Wait 29.1y</td><td>Wait 75.8y</td><td>Wait 92.9y</td><td>Wait 97.0y</td></tr><tr><td>Moderate (10%/yr)</td><td>Launch asap</td><td>Launch asap</td><td>Wait 2.6y</td><td>Wait 11.3y</td><td>Wait 15.8y</td><td>Wait 17.4y</td><td>Wait 17.8y</td></tr><tr><td>Brisk (50%/yr)</td><td>Launch asap</td><td>Wait 7.5m</td><td>Wait 2.6y</td><td>Wait 3.9y</td><td>Wait 1.1y</td></tr></tbody></table></figure><p>We see that some borderline cases shift from “launch immediately” to “wait a bit”; and cases that already warranted waiting now recommend longer delays. &nbsp;Higher discount rates would amplify this effect: if the far future counts for little, it makes sense to mostly focus on securing the near future.</p><h1>Quality of life adjustment</h1><p>One important hope is that developing superintelligence will not only extend life but also make it better. &nbsp;We can model this by assigning a quality weight&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">q</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-mn"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">0</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>&nbsp;to life before AGI and a higher weight&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">q</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-mn"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">1</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>&nbsp;to life after a successful AGI launch.</p><p>Table 5 shows optimal timing when post-AGI life is twice as good as current life (<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">q</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-mn"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">1</span></span></span></span><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mo"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">/</span></span></span></span><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span delay: small quality difference (q₁/q₀ = 2, medium discount rate&nbsp;</strong><span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">ρ</span></span><span class="mjx-mo MJXc-space3"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">=</span></span><span class="mjx-mn MJXc-space3"><span Progress</strong></td><td><strong>1%</strong></td><td><strong>5%</strong></td><td><strong>20%</strong></td><td><strong>50%</strong></td><td><strong>80%</strong></td><td><strong>95%</strong></td><td><strong>99%</strong></td></tr><tr><td>No 1.8y</td></tr><tr><td>Ultra-fast (99%/yr)</td><td>Wait 12.8d</td><td>Wait 4.6m</td><td>Wait 8.2m</td><td>Wait 10.6m</td><td>Wait 11.8m</td><td>Wait 1.0y</td><td>Wait 1.0y</td></tr></tbody></table></figure><p>We can see that higher post-AGI quality expands the “launch asap” region, and shortens delays in the instances where waiting is optimal.</p><p>The magnitude of this shift is limited because the “launch-asap” risk bar—the level of AGI-risk below which it becomes optimal to launch immediately—is bounded above. &nbsp;This means that the quality-effect saturates: even arbitrarily large quality improvements cannot push all cases to immediate launch. &nbsp;Thus, if we postulated that post-AGI life would be 1,000 or 10,000 times better than pre-AGI life, this would not make much difference compared to more modest levels of quality improvement. &nbsp;Intuitively, once post-AGI life becomes sufficiently attractive (because of its length and/or quality), pre-AGI life contributes relatively little to the expected value of the future; and the chief concern then becomes maximizing the chance of actually reaching the post-AGI era—i.e. balancing the improvements in AGI safety that come from waiting against the accumulating risk of dying before AGI if the wait is too long.</p><p>Interestingly, the effect of temporal discounting can flip sign depending on the magnitude of the pre/post-AGI quality differential. &nbsp;When there is no quality differential, higher temporal discount rates always push towards launching <i>later</i>. &nbsp;However, when there is a quality differential that is sufficiently large, impatience penalizes delaying the onset of the higher-quality existence that would follow a successful superintelligence; and this pulls towards launching earlier. &nbsp;Consequently, while discounting always acts as a brake in the pure longevity model, it acts as an accelerator when the quality-of-life gap is sufficiently large.</p><h1>Diminishing marginal utility</h1><p>The preceding models have relied on a linear value assumption—essentially treating a 1,400-year lifespan as subjectively worth exactly 35 times as much as a 40-year lifespan. &nbsp;However, most people’s actual current preferences may exhibit diminishing marginal utility in quality-adjusted lifeyears (QALYs), meaning that e.g. a ten-year extension of a life that would otherwise be, say, 30 years is regarded as more desirable than a ten-year extension of a life that would otherwise be 1,390 years. &nbsp;Such a preference structure can also be viewed as a form of risk-aversion. &nbsp;Few people would accept a coin flip where “heads” means doubling their remaining lifespan and “tails” means dying immediately—and they may reject it even if we introduce a modest sweetener (such as a $10,000 reward or an additional bonus lifeyear if the coin lands heads).</p><p>We can model this using a standard diminishing-returns utility function—constant relative risk aversion (CRRA)—that introduces a curvature parameter,&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">γ</span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, representing the degree of risk-aversion. &nbsp;As this parameter increases, the decision-maker becomes more conservative, requiring higher probabilities of success (or greater potential upside) before betting their current life on a transformation.</p><p>Table 6 shows the results for&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">γ</span></span><span class="mjx-mo MJXc-space3"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">=</span></span><span class="mjx-mn MJXc-space3"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">0.26</span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, a typical value derived from the empirical health-economics literature. &nbsp;Other parameters are the same as in the previous section. &nbsp;(See Appendix D for details and additional illustrations.)</p><p><strong>TABLE 6: Diminishing marginal utility (CRRA, medium rate)</strong></p><figure (0.1%/yr)</td><td>1.0%</td><td>5.0%</td><td>20.0%</td><td>49.9%</td><td>70.8%</td><td>70.8%</td><td>70.8%</td></tr><tr><td>Very slow (1%/yr)</td><td>1.0%</td><td>5.0%</td><td>20.0%</td><td>47.9%</td><td>58.1%</td><td>59.6%</td><td>59.9%</td></tr><tr><td>Moderate (10%/yr)</td><td>1.0%</td><td>5.0%</td><td>17.9%</td><td>20.6%</td><td>21.4%</td><td>21.6%</td><td>21.6%</td></tr><tr><td>Brisk (50%/yr)</td><td>1.0%</td><td>3.9%</td><td>4.1%</td><td>4.2%</td><td>4.2%</td><td>4.2%</td><td>4.2%</td></tr><tr><td>Very fast (90%/yr)</td><td>1.0%</td><td>1.3%</td><td>1.3%</td><td>1.3%</td><td>1.3%</td><td>1.3%</td><td>1.3%</td></tr><tr><td>Ultra-fast (99%/yr)</td><td>0.6%</td><td>0.6%</td><td>0.6%</td><td>0.6%</td><td>0.6%</td><td>0.6%</td><td>0.6%</td></tr></tbody></table></figure><p>These risk-at-launch values are somewhat—but not dramatically—reduced compared to those of a risk-neutral agent (except in cases where the risk-neutral agent would never launch or the risk-averse agent would launch asap, in which case risk-at-launch is the same for both).</p><h1>Changing rates of safety progress</h1><p>In the models considered so far, we assumed that AGI can be launched at any time, that background mortality remains constant until launch, that AI safety improves at a constant rate, and that no evidence about system safety is obtained beyond what that steady progress implies. &nbsp;In reality, however, we are not yet in a position to launch full AGI; background mortality risk could shift around the time AGI becomes available; the pace of safety progress is likely to vary across stages; and we may be able to run tests that provide direct information about whether a system is safe. &nbsp;We now explore how some of these factors affect the picture.</p><p>It is helpful to distinguish two timing variables:</p><ul><li><span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">agi</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>: the time from now until full AGI first becomes technically deployable. We will refer to this period as Phase 1.</li><li><span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">pause</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>: any additional delay we choose after that point before deploying—a deliberate pause between AGI becoming available and being rolled out at scale. We will refer to such a period as Phase 2.</li></ul><p>Launch thus occurs at time&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span><span class="mjx-mo MJXc-space3"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">=</span></span><span class="mjx-msubsup MJXc-space3"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">agi</span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mjx-mo MJXc-space2"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">+</span></span><span class="mjx-msubsup MJXc-space2"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">pause</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>.</p><p>In principle, one could try to choose both variables so as to maximize expected (discounted, quality-adjusted) life-years. &nbsp;In practice,&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">agi</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>&nbsp;may be harder to affect to a degree that makes a significant difference. &nbsp;It is largely determined by the inherent technical difficulty of attaining AGI-level capabilities and by investment choices currently driven by intense competitive dynamics; whereas&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">pause</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, in at least some scenarios, may be more a matter of deliberate choice by company leaders or policymakers who at that juncture may be more focused on making macrostrategically sound deployment decisions. &nbsp;Furthermore, as we shall see, relatively small changes to&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">pause</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>&nbsp;plausibly make a bigger difference to expected outcomes than similarly small changes to&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">agi</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>.</p><p>Before considering joint optimization over both variables, therefore, let us examine a model in which only&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">pause</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>&nbsp;is subject to choice. &nbsp;Here we treat &nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-msubsup"><span class="mjx-base"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I" style="padding-right: 0.12em;">T</span></span></span><span class="mjx-sub"><span class="mjx-texatom"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mtext"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">agi</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>&nbsp;as exogenous and given by the scenario (0, 5, 10, or 20 years until AGI availability). &nbsp;We retain the notation and parameters from previous sections, including exponential time discounting and concave utility (both at their “medium” values unless otherwise noted).</p><p>A key feature of this multiphase setup is that the rate of safety progress need not be constant. &nbsp;Different stages of development offer different opportunities for progress, and the most tractable problems tend to be solved first.</p><p>During Phase 1—the period before full AGI is available—safety researchers must work without access to the systems that will ultimately matter most. &nbsp;They can study precursor systems, develop theoretical frameworks, and devise alignment techniques that seem likely to scale; but the exact algorithms and architectures that enable full AGI remain unknown, limiting what can be tested or verified. &nbsp;Safety progress during this phase is therefore likely to be moderate.</p><p>The situation changes once AGI-ready systems are attained. &nbsp;In Phase 2, researchers can study the actual system, run it in constrained environments, probe its behavior under controlled conditions, and potentially leverage the system’s own capabilities to accelerate safety work. &nbsp;This suggests a burst of rapid safety progress immediately after AGI becomes available—a “safety windfall” from finally having the real artifact to work with.</p><p>Yet such rapid gains cannot continue indefinitely. &nbsp;The most promising interventions get explored first, and diminishing returns eventually set in. &nbsp;This motivates dividing Phase 2 into distinct subphases:</p><ul><li><i>Phase 2a</i>: An initial period of very rapid safety progress. With the full system now available, researchers can perform interventions that were previously impossible—shaping the system, probing failure modes while slowly ramping capabilities, and implementing oversight mechanisms on the actual weights. This subphase is brief (perhaps weeks to months) but highly productive.</li><li><i>Phase 2b</i>: Continued fast progress, though slower than 2a. The most obvious low-hanging fruit has been picked, but researchers still benefit from working on the actual system, assisted by advanced AI tools. This might last around a year.</li><li><i>Phase 2c</i>: Progress slows to a rate similar to Phase 1, the benefits of having the actual system now roughly offset by the depletion of tractable problems. This subphase might last several years.</li><li><i>Phase 2d</i>: Ultimately progress becomes very slow, consisting of fundamental research into alignment science or the development of qualitatively new architectures. This continues indefinitely.</li></ul><p>Figure 3 illustrates the qualitative picture. &nbsp;The key feature is that safety progress is front-loaded within Phase 2.</p><p><strong>Figure&nbsp;3. Qualitative picture of risk in a multiphase model</strong></p><p><strong><img -20.0y</td><td>Wait -19.7y</td><td>Wait -18.7y</td><td>Wait -15.9y</td><td>Wait -12.0y</td><td>Wait -10.5y</td><td>Wait -10.1y</td></tr></tbody></table></figure><p>We see that in many scenarios and for many initial levels of risk, if the decision-maker is free to jointly optimize over both AGI development time and subsequent pausing, it is optimal to launch earlier than would have happened by default: these are the cells with blue background. &nbsp;(In scenarios 1 and 2, acceleration is impossible since Phase 1 has zero duration.)</p><p>Additionally, there are several scenarios in which, although launch occurs in Phase 2 after some period of pausing, it is still optimal to accelerate to some extent in Phase 1: these are the cells that do not have blue background but do have blue borders. &nbsp;This can happen because the rate of risk reduction is faster in Phase 2a and 2b than during Phase 1. &nbsp;There is thus a special value in being able to pause for at least a short while after AGI-capability has been attained before deploying it; and it can be worth going faster through Phase 1 in order to harvest these rapid safety gains while still keeping the overall time until AGI deployment tolerably short.</p><h1>Shifting mortality rates</h1><p>We have been assuming a constant background mortality rate until the launch of AGI, yet it is conceivable that it could change around the time when AGI-capability is attained (but before it is fully deployed).</p><p>Pessimistically, the world might become more dangerous with the introduction of near-AGI capabilities. &nbsp;For example, specialized AI systems could proliferate the capability to produce (new and more lethal) bioweapons, enable vast swarms of autonomous drones, precipitate mayhem by destabilizing our individual or collective epistemic systems and political processes, or raise geopolitical stakes and urgency in such a way as to trigger major war.</p><p>Optimistically, one might hope that near-AGI systems would enable breakthroughs in medicine that reduce mortality rates. &nbsp;However, substantial mortality reductions seem unlikely to materialize quickly, since many medical innovations must pass through extensive clinical trials and then require further time to achieve globally significant scale. &nbsp;Near-AGI systems could, of course, also have many other positive effects; yet except possibly for medical applications, it seems unlikely that they would have a big immediate impact on average death rates, since most people who are currently dying are succumbing to age-related and other medical issues.</p><p>On balance, therefore, if there is a dramatic change in global mortality just around the time when AGI becomes possible, it seems likelier to be for the worse than for the better.&nbsp; This adds to the reasons for keeping wait times relatively short after AGI-capability (or near-AGI capability that starts having dangerous applications) has been attained.</p><p>Yet if&nbsp;a medical breakthrough <i>were</i>&nbsp;to emerge—and especially effective anti-aging therapies—then the optimal time to launch AGI could be pushed out considerably. &nbsp;In principle, such a breakthrough could come from either pre-AGI forms of AI (or specialized AGI applications that don’t require full deployment) or medical progress occurring independently of AI. &nbsp;Such developments are more plausible in long-timeline scenarios where AGI is not developed for several decades.</p><p>Note that for this effect to occur, it is not necessary for the improvement in background mortality to actually take place prior to or immediately upon entering Phase 2. &nbsp;In principle, the shift in optimal timelines could occur if an impending lowering of mortality becomes <i>foreseeable</i>;&nbsp;since this would immediately increase our <i>expected</i>&nbsp;lifespan under pre-launch conditions. &nbsp;For example, suppose we became confident that the rate of age-related decline will drop by 90% within 5 years (even without deploying AGI). &nbsp;It might then make sense to favor longer postponements—e.g. launching AGI in 50 years, when AI safety progress has brought the risk level down to a minimal level—since most of us could then still expect to be alive at that time. &nbsp;In this case, the 50 years of additional AI safety progress would be bought at the comparative bargain price of a death risk equivalent to waiting less than 10 years under current mortality conditions.</p><p>Table 10 shows the effects of postulating a precipitous drop in provide at least two types of benefit: first, it can improve the nature of an AI system so that it is less likely to cause catastrophic harm if deployed; second, it can provide information about that nature, so that we can better judge whether to deploy it or to keep working to make it safer. &nbsp;The previous sections modeled both effects with a single parameter (the “rate of AI safety progress”). &nbsp;If we are willing to tolerate a more complicated setup, we can instead treat them separately. &nbsp;This leads to models where what is determined in advance is not an optimal launch time but an optimal <i>policy</i>&nbsp;that specifies—conditional on whatever safety information is then available—whether to launch or to continue working and testing.</p><p>To keep the setup manageable, we graft a simple testing process onto the multiphase model from the previous section. &nbsp;Once AGI‑capable systems exist (the start of Phase 2), the true catastrophe probability at that time is unknown: it could be any of seven values, corresponding to the initial risk levels used earlier (1 %, 5 %, 20 %, 50 %, 80 %, 95 %, or 99 %). &nbsp;We assume a uniform prior over these possibilities. &nbsp;Safety work reduces the underlying risk over time following the same multiphase schedule as before: Phase 1 with moderate progress, followed (once AGI‑capable systems exist) by a brief period of very rapid safety improvement (Phase 2a), a somewhat slower but still fast phase (2b), a medium‑progress phase (2c), and then a long tail of very slow progress (2d).</p><p>Safety tests are triggered by safety progress rather than by clock time. &nbsp;Starting from the moment AGI‑capable systems are available, a new test is performed every time safety work has reduced the system’s intrinsic catastrophe probability by another 20 % relative to the last test. This reflects the idea that developing informative tests is itself part of safety work: as we make the system safer, we also learn how to probe it more effectively. &nbsp;If the underlying risk at the moment of testing is&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">p</span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, the test returns “fail” with probability&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mi"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">p</span></span></span></span></span></span></span>&nbsp;and “pass” with probability&nbsp;<span class="math-tex"><span class="mjpage"><span class="mjx-chtml"><span class="mjx-math"><span class="mjx-mrow"><span class="mjx-mn"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">1</span></span><span class="mjx-mo MJXc-space2"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-main-R">−</span></span><span class="mjx-mi MJXc-space2"><span class="mjx-char MJXc-TeX-math-I">p</span></span></span></span></span></span></span>. &nbsp;Systems with very high intrinsic riskiness therefore tend to fail tests repeatedly, whereas fairly safe systems mostly pass—even if their remaining risk is still substantial. &nbsp;In particular, these tests usually cannot distinguish reliably between, say, ten and twenty per cent risk at launch; they are better at separating “clearly terrible” from “not obviously terrible”.</p><p>We can formalize this setup as a partially observed Markov decision process (POMDP) and compute the optimal policy numerically (see Appendix G for details). &nbsp;Table 13 shows the expected delays (counting from the beginning of Phase 2).</p><p><strong>TABLE 13: Periodic safety tests</strong></p><figure
